steps: For charge: Q = I × t (coulombs = amperes × seconds)
For Ohm's law: V = IR. Rearrange to find I = V/R or R = V/I
Series total resistance: R_total = R1 + R2 + … Current is the same everywhere
Parallel circuits: pd is the same across every branch; total resistance is less than the smallest
method_card.title: Circuit Calculations
method_card.content:
Three equations cover all circuit calculations in this lesson.

Q = It: charge (C) = current (A) × time (s).

V = IR: potential difference (V) = current (A) × resistance (Ω). Always write the rearrangement explicitly before substituting.

Series vs Parallel — the most tested distinction:

  • Series: same current everywhere; pd splits across components; R_total = sum of all resistances.
  • Parallel: same pd across every branch; current splits; total resistance is less than any single branch.

Memory aid: 'Series Shares Voltage; Parallel Passes current equally.'

Common pitfalls:

  • Mixing up the current and pd rules for series/parallel
  • Not rearranging V = IR before substituting numbers

exam_context.frequency: High — circuit calculations appear in most physics papers

misconceptions.message: R_total = V ÷ I = 60 Ω. Subtract known resistances: R = 60 − 30 = 30 Ω.

gold.question: A thermistor in series with a 100 Ω fixed resistor is connected to a 6 V supply. The current is 0.03 A. Calculate the resistance of the thermistor.

misconceptions.message: R_total = V/I = 6/0.03 = 200 Ω. Thermistor R = 200 − 100 = 100 Ω.
Total resistance = V/I = 200 Ω. Thermistor = total − fixed = 100 Ω.

misconceptions.message: In parallel, pd across each branch = supply pd = 9 V. I1 = 9/30 = 0.3 A.
Parallel circuit — each branch has the full 9 V across it.
